title_en: Chen v. Wuxi Maternal and Child Health Hospital — dispute over medical service contract
ruling_gist_en: The husband and wife entered into a medical service contract for 'in vitro fertilization and embryo transfer' with a medical institution and had already completed contract contents such as egg retrieval and embryo culture. Before the formal embryo transfer, the husband died and had not indicated to the medical institution during his lifetime that he refused to perform the contract. The wife's request for the medical institution to continue performing the obligation of embryo transfer reflects the true intent of the parties, is also performable in content, and does not violate laws, regulations, or public order and good customs. Therefore, the medical institution should continue to perform the medical service contract.
keywords_en: Civil; Medical service contract dispute; First instance; Basic People's Court; Jiangsu Province; Natural person; Legal person; Civil Code; Continued performance of medical service contract; Conditions for embryo transfer surgery; Reproductive rights of widowed women; Support the plaintiff; In vitro fertilization and embryo transfer (IVF-ET); Husband's death; Embryo cryopreservation; Medical institution's refusal to transfer; Public order and good customs; Good faith; Contract dispute; Service contract; Dispute over medical service contract with maternal and child health hospital
full_text_en:
Chen v. Wuxi Maternal and Child Health Care Hospital — dispute over medical service contract

Ruling Summary

Where a married couple enters into a medical service contract for "in vitro fertilization-embryo transfer" with a medical institution, and the contract has already been partially performed including egg retrieval and embryo culture, and the husband dies before the formal embryo transfer without having expressed to the medical institution any refusal to perform the contract, the wife's request that the medical institution continue to perform the embryo transfer obligation reflects the true intent of the parties, is capable of being performed, does not violate laws, regulations, or public order and good customs, and the medical institution shall continue to perform the medical service contract.

Where a widowed woman, in compliance with relevant national population and family planning laws and regulations, seeks to continue to bear a child using embryos obtained through the implementation of assisted reproductive technology by her and her husband, this is distinct from the "single woman" referred to in the former Ministry of Health's Technical Standards for the Implementation of Human Assisted Reproductive Technology, and does not violate the principle of social welfare. A hospital may not rely on administrative regulations in the form of departmental rules to oppose a party's legitimate reproductive rights under the law.

Plaintiff: Chen, female, born on May 8, 1994, Han ethnicity, residing in Quanjiao County, Anhui Province.

Defendant: Wuxi Maternal and Child Health Care Hospital, domiciled at Huaishu Lane, Liangxi District, Wuxi City, Jiangsu Province.

Legal Representative: Yang Yaping, President of the Hospital.

The plaintiff, Chen, brought an action before the Liangxi District People's Court of Wuxi City, Jiangsu Province, against the defendant, Wuxi Maternal and Child Health Care Hospital (hereinafter referred to as the Maternal and Child Health Hospital), regarding a dispute over a medical service contract.

The plaintiff, Chen, alleged as follows: In August 2016, she and her husband, Li, consulted the Maternal and Child Health Hospital for infertility and requested the performance of an "in vitro fertilization-embryo transfer" procedure. The couple underwent egg retrieval and sperm retrieval at the Maternal and Child Health Hospital respectively, and embryos were successfully cultivated, but the subsequent embryo transfer procedure was unsuccessful. On May 26, 2017, the couple again attended the Maternal and Child Health Hospital requesting an "in vitro fertilization-embryo transfer" procedure, and four embryos were successfully cultivated, scheduled to be transferred into her body in July 2017. However, because she had developed ascites due to the retrieval of a large number of eggs, it was not suitable to immediately transfer the embryos. She recuperated at home, intending to undergo the transfer procedure when her physical condition was suitable. On July 1, 2019, her husband, Li, died in an accident. Thereafter, she requested the Maternal and Child Health Hospital to continue and complete the "in vitro fertilization-embryo transfer" procedure, but the Maternal and Child Health Hospital refused on the grounds that Li's signature was lacking and that the procedure could not be performed in accordance with relevant regulations. Her husband was the only son of the family, and the couple had a good relationship during their marriage. Although she was widowed, continuing the embryo transfer procedure to carry on her husband's bloodline embodied the entire hope of herself and her parents-in-law. She requested the court to order the Maternal and Child Health Hospital to continue to perform the medical service contract for "in vitro fertilization-embryo transfer" between the two parties, to perform the embryo transfer procedure for her, and to bear the litigation costs of this case.

The defendant, the Maternal and Child Health Hospital, argued as follows: 1. According to the provisions of the "Technical Standards for Human Assisted Reproductive Technology" (Wei Ke Jiao [2001] No. 143) and the "Ethical Principles for Human Assisted Reproductive Technology," assisted reproductive technology must strictly adhere to the voluntary principle of informed consent and informed choice. Chen's husband, Li, had not undergone embryo transfer surgery in the two years prior to his death. The informed consent signed by Li during his lifetime could not extend beyond his death, and Li could no longer sign the informed consent for embryo thawing and transfer. Chen's claim for continued performance of the contract contradicts legal provisions. 2. In April 2017, when Chen and her husband signed the consent form for embryo freezing, thawing, and transfer, they were clearly informed that the initial freezing fee included three months of embryo preservation fees. If continued freezing was required beyond the deadline, additional fees must be paid, otherwise the embryos would not be preserved. If the preservation period was exceeded, they agreed to de-identify the embryos and use them for teaching and scientific research. However, after paying the initial embryo freezing fee, Chen never paid the freezing fees for more than two years beyond the preservation period. Chen's failure to attend for embryo transfer surgery at the hospital for two years before her husband's death, without cause, constituted a subjective abandonment of the embryos. Chen's failure to undergo the surgery without justifiable reason was the fundamental reason for the non-performance of the contract. 3. After Li's death, Chen became a single woman. A single-parent environment may have impacts on the child's physical, psychological, and personality development. According to the principles of protecting offspring and public welfare under the "Technical Standards for Human Assisted Reproductive Technology," the hospital cannot perform assisted reproductive technology for a single woman, nor does it recommend assisted reproductive technology for a single woman. Chen is no longer a suitable subject for the application of human assisted reproductive technology. The hospital cannot perform the thawing and transfer of frozen embryos for Chen, and requests that Chen's claim be dismissed.

The Liangxi District People's Court of Wuxi City, Jiangsu Province, found the following facts at first instance:

The defendant, the Maternal and Child Health Hospital, is a licensed medical institution approved by the health administrative department to carry out human assisted reproductive technology. The plaintiff, Chen, and her husband, Li, registered their marriage on January 6, 2015. Starting in August 2016, Chen and Li attended the Maternal and Child Health Hospital for diagnosis and treatment of infertility due to tubal factors in the wife. On December 18, 2016, the Maternal and Child Health Hospital performed an "in vitro fertilization-embryo transfer" procedure on Chen, but Chen did not become pregnant. On April 27, 2017, Chen and Li again attended the Maternal and Child Health Hospital requesting IVF-ET, i.e., an "in vitro fertilization-embryo transfer" procedure to assist pregnancy. The proposed plan by the Maternal and Child Health Hospital was: stimulation cycle, ultra-long protocol. On that same day, Chen and Li signed an "Informed Consent for In Vitro Fertilization-Embryo Transfer" with the Maternal and Child Health Hospital, agreeing to authorize the hospital to diagnose and treat their infertility and voluntarily choosing "in vitro fertilization-embryo transfer." On May 28, 2017, the Maternal and Child Health Hospital performed egg retrieval and sperm retrieval procedures on Chen and Li respectively, and carried out embryo culture. On the same day, Chen showed a tendency toward ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome. The Maternal and Child Health Hospital administered volume expansion treatment and froze all embryos. The Maternal and Child Health Hospital posted a "Notice on Transfer Procedure" in Chen's medical records, which stated: "1. At 07:30 on _ month _ day, the couple should come to the hospital. The wife should register. Both parties should bring the original marriage certificate, ID card, and birth permit. Come to the Reproductive Center (Room 607) and wait patiently for the medical staff to arrange to view the embryo list. After viewing, both parties sign. Then the nurse verifies the evidence and issues the fee items. Transfer fee: RMB 2,200 + 30, assisted hatching: RMB 1,200. Embryo freezing continuation fee: RMB 150/month. ... Special reminder: For frozen embryo transfer, before embryo thawing, both parties should come to Room 607 at 13:30 on _ month _ day to sign. Thawing fee: RMB 800. Embryo full freeze preservation continuation fee: RMB 150/month." The words "special reminder" and "both parties" were in bold typeface and relatively conspicuous. On June 2, 2017, Chen was admitted to the Maternal and Child Health Hospital with chest and abdominal effusion, diagnosed with ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome and post-egg retrieval. On June 3, 2017, Chen and Li signed an "Informed Consent for Embryo Freezing, Thawing, and Transfer" with the Maternal and Child Health Hospital, which stated: "Chen and Li declare that they have undergone IVF, i.e., in vitro fertilization, at the Maternal and Child Health Hospital. Currently, there are 2 cleavage-stage embryos and 2 blastocysts remaining. They request that the Maternal and Child Health Hospital preserve these embryos using low-temperature preservation technology. They understand that the initial freezing fee includes three months of embryo preservation fees. If continued freezing is required beyond the deadline, additional fees must be paid, otherwise the embryos will not be preserved. If the preservation period is exceeded, they agree to de-identify the embryos and use them for teaching and scientific research." On June 7, 2017, Chen's condition improved and she was discharged. The discharge order stated that Chen should attend the outpatient clinic of the Reproductive Center of the Maternal and Child Health Hospital within one week and follow up as needed. Thereafter, due to physical reasons, Chen did not attend the Maternal and Child Health Hospital for consultation or embryo transfer, and also failed to pay the frozen embryo preservation fees. Currently, 2 cleavage-stage embryos and 2 blastocysts remain cryopreserved at the Maternal and Child Health Hospital, and the Maternal and Child Health Hospital has not changed the original preservation method or conditions for these frozen embryos and blastocysts. In addition, during the process of requesting the "in vitro fertilization-embryo transfer" procedure for assisted pregnancy at the Maternal and Child Health Hospital on April 27, 2017, Chen and Li also signed a "Commitment Letter," "Informed Consent for Blastocyst Culture," "Informed Consent for Selective Single Embryo Transfer," "Informed Consent for Selective Single Blastocyst Transfer," "Informed Consent for the Disposition of Gametes and Embryos," etc.

On July 1, 2019, Li died unexpectedly. Thereafter, the plaintiff, Chen, went to the Maternal and Child Health Hospital requesting continued performance of the medical service contract to perform the embryo transfer procedure, but was refused by the defendant, the Maternal and Child Health Hospital.

On October 9, 2019, the plaintiff, Chen, filed this lawsuit with the court. During the proceedings, Li's father, Li A, and mother, Liu B, both appeared in court and stated that they had three sons, with Li being the youngest, and his two older brothers had already passed away. Now Li had also died unexpectedly. As parents, they were aware that Li had previously sought artificial assisted reproduction at the hospital. They supported their daughter-in-law, Chen, in continuing with the embryo transfer procedure, hoping to continue Li's bloodline and give the living some hope. They agreed to assume the legal rights and obligations arising from the birth of a child after Chen's embryo transfer, including ethical and moral obligations. Chen's father, Chen C, also appeared in court and clearly supported his daughter's claim. Chen stated in court that she operates a beauty salon and has a certain income, and she promised to assume the ethical, moral, and legal rights and obligations after the embryo transfer and childbirth. In addition, the Health and Family Planning Office of Wugang Town, Quanjiao County, Chuzhou City, Anhui Province, where Chen's household registration is located, and the Guandu Village Committee of Wugang Town, Quanjiao County, Chuzhou City, Anhui Province, issued a written certificate to the court stating that Chen and Li complied with the national family planning policy and had never given birth to or adopted children.

It was further found that after Chen was admitted to the Maternal and Child Health Hospital for ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome following egg retrieval, she consulted the defendant, the Maternal and Child Health Hospital, about whether the frozen embryo preservation fees could be paid together with the later embryo transfer. The medical staff of the Maternal and Child Health Hospital agreed. During the proceedings, Chen telephoned the attending physician and head nurse of the Maternal and Child Health Hospital to inquire about paying the overdue frozen embryo preservation fees. She was informed that as long as the couple had not jointly signed to destroy the embryos, the frozen embryos would not be destroyed or used for scientific research and would continue to be preserved according to normal procedures. She was also clearly informed that it was acceptable to pay the frozen embryo preservation fees later, simply by coming to the hospital, registering, and seeing the doctor to pay the preservation fees. Later, she was informed that because a civil lawsuit was currently pending between the parties, she should wait until the court confirmed that the embryo transfer procedure could be performed before paying the frozen embryo preservation fees. During the trial of this case, Chen paid RMB 5,550, being the overdue frozen embryo preservation fees up to July 2020, into the court for deposit.

The Liangxi District People's Court of Wuxi City, Jiangsu Province, held at first instance:

The plaintiff, Chen, and her husband, Li, attended the defendant, the Maternal and Child Health Hospital, which is approved by the health administrative department and registered to carry out human assisted reproductive technology, for human assisted reproductive treatment due to infertility. The Maternal and Child Health Hospital cultivated and froze embryos for them. The medical service contract relationship formed between the two parties is lawful and valid. The dispute in this case is whether, after Li's death, Chen's request to continue with the embryo transfer procedure violates relevant ethics and morals, whether it conforms to the contract and legal provisions, and whether the relevant medical service contract between the doctor and patient should continue to be performed.

The "Administrative Measures for Human Assisted Reproductive Technology" promulgated by the former Ministry of Health in February 2001, and the "Technical Standards for Human Assisted Reproductive Technology" and "Ethical Principles for Human Assisted Reproductive Technology and Human Sperm Banks" issued by the former Ministry of Health in May 2001 and subsequently revised in June 2003, respectively provide that: the implementation of human assisted reproductive technology shall comply with the provisions of the "Technical Standards for Human Assisted Reproductive Technology"; the implementation of human assisted reproductive technology shall follow the principle of informed consent and sign an informed consent form; practitioners of human assisted reproductive technology are prohibited from providing human assisted reproductive technology to couples who do not comply with the national population and family planning laws and regulations and to single women; human assisted reproductive technology shall follow the ethical principle of protecting offspring. In this case, although the defendant, the Maternal and Child Health Hospital, sympathized with the plaintiff's situation, it refused Chen's request for continued performance of the medical service contract out of a rigorous and cautious medical practice and based on the relevant administrative measures and ethical principles formulated by the former Ministry of Health, and raised these as a defense in this lawsuit. In this regard, the court held that: First, the purpose of the medical service contract between Chen and her husband Li and the Maternal and Child Health Hospital was to have a child. Although Chen's husband Li had died, the facts that Li and Chen jointly underwent two courses of human assisted reproductive technology treatment at the Maternal and Child Health Hospital during his lifetime, and in particular signed multiple informed consent forms in this medical service contract and had embryos cultivated and frozen, all demonstrate Li's clear intent to have a child through human assisted reproductive technology, and it can be inferred that continuing the embryo transfer procedure does not violate Li's intent during his lifetime. During the performance of the human assisted reproductive technology procedure by the Maternal and Child Health Hospital for Chen and Li, Li's views on embryo freezing, thawing, and transfer had been confirmed by a blanket, general signature on the informed consent form. The reason why the embryo transfer was not immediately performed was solely due to Chen's physical condition. The existing medical service contract had not yet been completed, and there were still embryos preserved at the Maternal and Child Health Hospital for the couple. Chen, as one of the patient parties, unilaterally requested the Maternal and Child Health Hospital to continue to perform the medical service contract that she and her husband had long since entered into with the hospital. This does not violate the true expression of the parties' intent or the principle of informed consent. The Maternal and Child Health Hospital, based on the pathological factors of Chen's infertility and the current family situation, and from the perspective of protecting the legal right to bear children and the ethical principle of benefiting the patient, should not rigidly adhere to the formality that Li did not sign at the time of embryo transfer under the existing medical service contract. Li's failure to sign does not necessarily constitute an obstacle to continued performance. Second, although a child born would not have a biological father and might grow up in a single-parent family, this hypothetical condition does not necessarily mean there will be serious impacts on the child's physical, psychological, or personality development. There is currently no evidence that the implementation of human assisted reproductive technology would lead to adverse consequences for offspring in terms of medicine, parental rights, or other aspects. Furthermore, children born through human assisted reproductive technology enjoy the same legal rights and assume the same legal obligations as children born naturally, including family ethics and moral obligations. Chen's request to continue with the human assisted reproductive technology procedure has obtained the consent of Li's parents and the support of her own father, and they are willing to assume legal obligations including moral and ethical ones. Therefore, the continued performance of human assisted reproductive technology for Chen by the Maternal and Child Health Hospital does not violate the principle of protecting offspring. Third, Chen and Li had no children and had not adopted any children. Chen's desire to bear a child does not violate relevant national population and family planning laws and regulations. Although Li has died, Chen, as a widowed woman, is now requesting to continue to bear a child using embryos obtained through the implementation of human assisted reproductive technology by her and her husband. This is distinct from the "single woman" referred to in the above administrative regulations of the former Ministry of Health who requests the implementation of human assisted reproductive technology. Therefore, Chen's request that the Maternal and Child Health Hospital continue to transfer embryos for her does not violate the principle of social welfare. Furthermore, the above regulations of the former Ministry of Health are administrative provisions for relevant medical institutions and personnel when engaging in artificial assisted reproductive technology. The Maternal and Child Health Hospital may not rely on administrative regulations in the form of departmental rules to oppose a party's legitimate reproductive rights under civil law.

During the litigation, the Defendant, the Maternal and Child Health Hospital (hereinafter "the Hospital"), argued that the Plaintiff, Chen, had failed to pay the overdue fees for the preservation of frozen embryos and had not returned to the Hospital for embryo transfer surgery for two years without reason, which constituted a subjective abandonment of the embryos and was the fundamental cause of the non-performance of the contract. Chen contended that the provisions in the informed consent form regarding "the initial freezing fee, continuing freezing fees, and preservation period..." constituted standard terms, which were subject to different interpretations, and that the Hospital had not fulfilled its duty to provide explanations and reminders. Therefore, Chen argued that the terms should be interpreted in favor of the patient in accordance with the law. Chen claimed that the overdue frozen embryo preservation fees would be paid at the time of embryo transfer, which was also an industry practice, and that the preservation period should be understood as the medical "shelf life of 5-10 years." Even if it were not a standard term, the Hospital should have sent a reminder to Chen to pay the fees, given that Chen had suffered significant physical and mental harm from the assisted reproduction treatments and had incurred substantial upfront costs, and would not abandon the embryos merely because of an overdue preservation fee of RMB 150 per month, nor did Chen have any intention of abandoning the embryo transfer. In response, the court held that the provision agreed upon by the medical parties—"the patient acknowledges that the initial freezing fee includes three months of embryo preservation fees. If the patient wishes to continue freezing beyond this period, the patient must pay the additional fees; otherwise, preservation will not be continued. If the preservation period is exceeded, the patient agrees to have the embryos de-identified and used for teaching and scientific research purposes"—constituted a standard term. The provision did not specify a clear time limit for the overdue payment of fees. The Hospital's "Transplant Instructions" indicated that the frozen embryo preservation fee was to be paid on the day of the transplant surgery, and the recording of Chen's conversation with the Hospital's medical staff corroborated that the Hospital had agreed to allow Chen to pay the frozen embryo preservation fees together with the later embryo transfer fees. Regarding the term "preservation period" in the provision, the medical parties also had different interpretations. If, as the Hospital argued, the preservation period meant three months or the period for which the patient paid the freezing fees, then according to that provision, once the three-month or fee-paying period was exceeded, the embryos would be directly used for de-identified teaching and scientific research, and there would be no situation requiring continued freezing and payment of fees. Therefore, the "preservation period" in this provision could not be automatically understood as the period for which the embryo preservation fees were paid. In accordance with the provisions of the Contract Law, where a standard term has two or more interpretations, the interpretation unfavorable to the party providing the standard term shall prevail. Accordingly, the term should be understood as the "shelf life" of the frozen embryos as interpreted by the patient, and the Hospital could not infer from this standard term that Chen had subjectively abandoned the frozen embryos. Although the Hospital's "Transplant Instructions" and the discharge instructions for Chen's treatment for ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome advised Chen to attend the reproductive center clinic one week later, neither document specified a clear time for embryo transfer, and the Hospital had not agreed on any time limit for Chen's embryo transfer surgery. Even if the conditions for contract rescission were met, the Hospital had not exercised its right to rescind the contract. The Hospital's defense during the litigation—that the contract had been rescinded—in order to counter Chen's claim for continued performance of the contract, violated the principle of good faith and conflicted with the court's exercise of adjudicative power. Therefore, the Hospital's assertion of the right to rescind the contract during the litigation could not produce legal effect. From the conversation between Chen and the Hospital's medical staff during the litigation regarding the inquiry about paying the overdue frozen embryo preservation fees, the Hospital agreed to allow Chen to register and pay the overdue embryo freezing fees. This should also be deemed a waiver of the right to rescind the contract, and thus the medical service contract between the medical parties had not been rescinded. Furthermore, the Hospital had not taken any factual disposition of the frozen embryos due to Chen's non-payment of the preservation fees. In fact, the four embryos were still being cryopreserved under the original conditions. There was no situation in which the Hospital was factually unable to perform. After Chen deposited the frozen embryo preservation fees with the court, Chen insisted on the performance of the existing medical service contract, which was consistent with the contract agreement between the medical parties and the legal provisions.

In summary, a contract lawfully formed is legally binding on the parties, and both parties shall perform their respective obligations in accordance with the contract. The Plaintiff, Chen's, request that the Defendant, the Hospital, continue to perform the medical service contract and carry out embryo transfer for Chen reflected the true intent of the parties, was capable of being performed, did not violate laws, regulations, or public order and good customs. Therefore, Chen's claim was supported. The Hospital's defense arguments were not adopted.

Accordingly, the Liangxi District People's Court of Wuxi, Jiangsu Province, in accordance with Article 3 of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China, Article 8(1), Article 60(1), and Article 107 of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China, and Article 17 of the Law of the People's Republic of China on Population and Family Planning, rendered the following judgment on June 23, 2020:

Wuxi Maternal and Child Health Hospital shall continue to perform the "in vitro fertilization-embryo transfer" medical service contract with Chen and carry out embryo transfer surgery for Chen, effective from the date this judgment becomes legally effective.

After the judgment of first instance was rendered, neither party appealed within the statutory period, and the judgment of first instance has become legally effective.
